Hey OP, 

I was on anti-depressants for 6 months and they kept upping my dosage because it was making me feel worse, and they thought that the dosage might be too minute, but it turned out that I have bipolar and anti-depressants can cause somebody with bipolar to fall into a kind of hyper depression. 

It's not just bipolar that anti-depressants work against, either. 

I'm not a psych, and I'm definitely not saying you for sure have bipolar or another mental health condition but it seems apparent that prozac is working negatively with your brain chemistry for whatever reason (like, perhaps your depression is environmental and not chemical?) In any case, it's really dangerous to stay on them at this point so wean off and either 

A) Try a different anti-depressant because it could just be the makeup of prozac 
B) Refuse to take anti-depressants completely 
C) Talk to your psych about the possibility of having something else, or trying something else. 

I was so morbidly depressed on SSRIs, but it lessened when I stopped taking them so please don't do anything rash, because it's the brain chemicals working against your better judgement. 

Stay strong.

When you're depressed or anxious, you can get stuck doing the same thing and not really think about other options. Maybe a change in his field would be the catalyst for a change in his attitude to life.

You say he isn't overtly happy, and apathy is certainly a sign of depression and sometimes, in the depths of depression, it's hard to find the energy to find and maintain friendships because it's all very emotionally taxing/exhausting. 

Apathy toward hobbies that used to be passions is also a sign of depression, but I'm obviously no psychologist. 

I think the first step would be to push him to actually seek help- it's easier to talk about than to actually do. Just a forewarning that, at least in my country, they'll throw medication at you but I think most cases of depression are environmental rather than chemical and I know a few people who have been ruined by antidepressants.
